messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David is a 58-year-old dentist who came to treatment after more than a year of feeling as if his life had narrowed into something tense, watchful, and unrecognizable. The trauma he returns to began after he was pulled over driving home from his practice one evening. He describes it as an ordinary stop that turned violent with a speed he still cannot fully comprehend. He remembers an officer shouting at him to keep his hands visible, then another voice cutting across it, louder and closer, and being yanked from the car before he understood what he had done wrong. He was forced onto the pavement, his face turned to the side, his chest pinned down, and he felt sharp pain through his shoulder and ribs. What stayed with him most vividly were the sounds—the barked commands, the radio crackling, the metallic clatter near his ear—and the bodily pain of being pressed down while he tried to say he was a doctor, that he was cooperating. No apology followed, and no meaningful accountability came afterward. David had come to believe there was something about him that made this happen, something in him that had marked him out to be treated that way, and at the same time he was consumed by the conviction that it was deeply unjust and that nothing had been done about it. He speaks of that contradiction with bitterness: he knows it was wrong, yet he still feels, at some level, that he must have invited it.

In the months after, the memory did not settle into the past. It often came back in a way that felt strange and disconnected, as if it belonged to somebody else and not to him. At other times it arrived with brutal sensory force: he would hear the officer’s voice in his head with startling clarity, or feel pain in his shoulder and side in the same places that had hurt on the pavement. Those returns seemed to confirm his bleakest conclusions. When the sounds and pain came back so vividly, he took it as proof that the incident had ruined his life and permanently altered him; the fact that the memory felt alien only deepened his fear that something fundamental in him had been broken.

His work as a dentist has become one of the main places where this pattern plays out. He still goes to the office, but he is preoccupied with where people are in relation to him. If a new patient or delivery person comes in unexpectedly, he feels a jolt of threat that far exceeds the situation, especially when a stranger approaches him quickly in a hallway or waiting area. In meetings he chooses the chair with the clearest view of the door and the easiest exit, and in restaurants after work he does the same. He sleeps badly, often lying awake for hours, listening for sounds in the house and mentally tracking where every person is. This persistent sense that danger could come from ordinary strangers keeps him scanning faces, entrances, posture, tone of voice. That constant vigilance leaves him exhausted and keyed up, and in that state the memory is easier to trigger; a man raising his voice in the parking lot outside the clinic, or the clipped authority in a security guard’s speech, can bring back the shouted commands and the pain in his body almost immediately. The more often this happens, the more certain David becomes that the world is not safe and that the police assault destroyed the life he used to have.

To manage this, David has steadily organized his days around avoidance. He tries not to feel much of anything at all, not only fear and anger but also excitement or pleasure, because any strong emotion seems capable of opening the door to the memory. He avoids stressful situations whenever he can, delegates difficult conversations at the practice, leaves crowded places early, and turns down social invitations from friends he once enjoyed seeing. When he cannot avoid being out, he checks his surroundings constantly. These strategies make sense to him in the moment: if he stays numb, if he keeps life small, if he notices every possible threat before it reaches him, perhaps he can prevent the memory from taking over again. But the cost has been cumulative. The more he constricts his life and monitors the environment, the more the trauma stays active in his mind; his efforts to suppress it seem only to make the sounds and bodily pain return more abruptly, and each return reinforces his view that he has been permanently damaged. His partner has told him he seems absent even when sitting in the same room, always half-listening for something else, and David hears that as further evidence that the trauma has already taken too much.

By the time he sought help, what finally frightened him was not only the intensity of the memories but the feeling that he was disappearing behind them. He was still going to the dental office, still functioning on the surface, but he felt increasingly certain that strangers were dangerous, that he could not let himself relax, and that his life had been derailed beyond repair. He says he wants help because he cannot keep living as if every room must be assessed for escape and every emotion shut down. What he fears most is that this is now who he is, and what he hopes, cautiously, is that the memory might someday feel like his past rather than an attack that keeps happening in the present.
